entries.title: b-side books
entries.shortDescription: B-sides is an ongoing series of artist books assembled from collections of found images accumulated over many years.
entries.fullText: B-sides is an ongoing series of small and affordable artist books that I make from the image collections I have accumulated over the years. Working with image sets gathered around shared subjects, the books explore how repeated photographs begin to function as vernacular working documents, revealing the conventions, omissions and contradictions that emerge as images circulate. Through editing, sequencing, cropping and reproduction, each publication becomes both an experiment in the book form and a way of making sense of image archives that continue to grow through use.

entries.title: reflections impressions
entries.shortDescription: solo presentation about 二泉映月, Erquan Yingyue and 阿炳 Abing | Esplanade Community Wall, Singapore
entries.fullText:
Drawing from her personal experience of learning and teaching the erhu, 印映 reflections impressions by Hong Shu-ying unfurls through an ensemble of works encompassing video, print and annotations to reflect on imitation and mimicking as a way of learning. At the source of these works lies the famed 1950 erhu audio recording of Mirrored Moon in the Erquan Spring (二泉映月, Erquan Yingyue) by Abing. A seminal figure in the realm of the erhu, Abing is a Chinese folk musician revered for his innovative playing style and legendary—but largely undocumented —contributions to musical compositions for this two-stringed bowed instrument.

Despite its poor audio quality, Abing’s 1950 recording of Mirrored Moon in the Erquan Spring served as the reference for transcribing the erhu classic into cipher notation (or jianpu), evolving into a systematic method for disseminating and learning the composition. Subsequently, performance recordings and user-made videos of the piece have been created, owing to its widespread popularity, considerable significance within cultural contexts, and its role as a valuable resource for learning and instructing the erhu. Intrigued by the proliferation of these recordings, this exhibition sees Hong delving into videos of Mirrored Moon in the Erquan Spring by both professionals and amateurs of erhu on platforms like YouTube and Youku. Through processes of cropping and screenshotting various lunar and hand imagery as well as representations of Abing, Hong extracts the parallels and variations in these materials, observing how they imagine, shapeshift and form diverse timecapsules of expressions. 

Finally, undergirding the works is the significance of notations and annotations in learning and playing the erhu. These annotations offer a comprehensive guide, providing technical and interpretational insights essential for learning a piece. For Hong, they also act as a conduit for the transmission and preservation by establishing an informal lineage from erhu teachers and other performers, as well as fostering a continuum of understanding and interpretation.

-

The entire series is an on-going project with further plans to develop it into a book. The audio component, [title]再现依心曲 ad lib[/title] can be found [here](https://shu0shushu.bandcamp.com/album/ad-lib).

entries.title: How We Learn(t)
entries.shortDescription: award showcase for Kwek Leng Joo Prize of Excellence in Photography, curated by Berny Tan | Gillman Barracks, Singapore

credits.name: Kwek Leng Joo Prize of Excellence in Photography
NTU ADM, Ang Song Nian, Muhammad Mustajab Bin Mohamad

entries.fullText:
[title]How We Learn(t)[/title] brings together two new bodies of work that examine, deconstruct, and re-present existing systems of knowledge.

Informed by her eighteen years as a member of various Chinese orchestras, Hong Shu-ying reflects on the culture of ensembleship in 「 濡 睦 」 resonations. Exploring hand-copied scores, pre-concert tuning, and orchestral seating arrangements, her works illuminate the shared languages and collective experiences that live on the periphery, yet serve as the scaffolding for communal music-making.

In substance of a minute, recorded by a machine and a few others, Syahrul Anuar takes the tools, techniques, and visual vocabulary of cartography into his own hands, removing them from positions of authority and perceived objectivity. Through four exercises in which mapmaking is unlearned and relearned, he challenges the seemingly immutable frameworks that govern the way we move through urban Singapore.

Recipients of the Kwek Leng Joo Prize of Excellence in Photography 2021, the two artists sidestep conventional photography in this exhibition. In its place are sculptures, moving images, and prints resembling drawings, all of which deliberately skirt the bodies of knowledge at the heart of their subjects.

Still, the ‘documentative’—one of the core functions of photography—remains insistently present in both series. It has been reimagined as gestures that are abstract, speculative, intimate, and reflexive; gestures that dislocate something from its source, in order to transform our understanding.

See the [catalogue](https://bernytan.com/s/HowWeLearnt_Catalogue_DigitalPreview_Artworks.pdf).

entries.title: collecting cipher
entries.shortDescription: solo presentation about hand-copied and annotated scores exhibiting artist | 窯座 Yao Alternative Art Space, Taichung

credits.name: 窯座 Yao Alternative Art Space, Taichung

entries.fullText:
I started playing the erhu in an orchestra when I was 7 years old. This experience gave me 20 years to observe the customs, gestures, and behaviours of communal music-making from within. The concept of a Chinese orchestra as we know it today is a relatively recent development in the history of Chinese instrumental music, with much of the traditions and customs still being formed.

In my teenage years, I served as a score librarian for 5 years, which explains my penchant for hand-copied jianpu (cypher notation). The jianpu is accessible and symbolic of the shared languages and collective experiences on the periphery. The various handwriting and symbols created and borrowed are also full of stories and allusions of their own. As a mnemonic device, jianpu is almost like a language system, serving as the scaffolding for communal music-making. These inconspicuous notes are all traces of learning, adaptation, innovation and sharing; embedded in them is the culture of ensembleship with curious quirks, rooted in a desire to carve out a shared language and identity.

The works presented in [title]彼觸 collecting ciphers[/title] manifests the different stories found within the annotations and handwritten elements of these hand-copied notations and scores.

See the [show collateral](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1tXCGpEsqlHeI4ACG-BSKVuqzijiF7wvk/view?usp=sharing) or listen to [窑谣 240407_yaoyao](https://shu0shushu.bandcamp.com/album/240407-yaoyao), an alternative documentation.

entries.title: Part Time Book Club
entries.shortDescription: Two friends’ attempt to discover and share (art)books, realising there’s simply not enough time to uncover them all on our own.
entries.fullText:
PTBC villian origin story

Part Time Book Club (PTBC) began in November 2024 as a spontaneous initiative between two friends, Shu and Ming, sparked by a simple truth: there are far too many good art books out there in the world, and not enough time to discover them alone. What began as a shared curiosity has since grown into a community-powered space where art book lovers come together to connect and uncover new titles. PTBC gatherings typically take the form of ad-hoc gatherings focused on the sharing and discovery of (art) books.

PTBC also aims to question inherited ideas of what books are and how they move through the world — exploring alternative modes of production, distribution, and discovery beyond conventional systems like mainstream bookstores and libraries, turning instead to independent publishers, informal networks, and ground-up libraries.

entries.title: |​​      | on paper
entries.shortDescription: Marks, spacing, and parallel pauses registered across paper sheets.
entries.fullText:
[title]|​​      | on paper[/title] is an experimental ‘residency’ that begins with a letter and four sheets of A4 paper. Instead of a studio with four walls, the project provides four sheets of A4 paper as the artists’ material and/or “studio space.” These simple materials serve as the site for artistic exploration and creation—the papers can function both as workspace and medium.

Once the four sheets of A4 paper have reached the artists, they are free to work with them in any way imaginable. They could draw or paint, poke or fold, sculpt or scan, cut or tear, and make with/on the paper in any way they wish.

The final showcase will act as a ‘library’ and ‘archive’. Each piece of paper exhibited offers a glimpse into an artist's world and unique point-of-view, and offers some insight into their artistic practice and journey. These works will be accompanied by letters written by the co-initiators and the artists.

entries.shortDescription: in the aisle gathers photographs, textures and overheard conversations from Chinese supermarkets in Edinburgh.

Installation view at [title]Bearings[/title] (2019), ADM Gallery, Singapore.

Installation view at [title]Bearings[/title] (2019), ADM Gallery, Singapore.

Made during a two-week programme while living away from Singapore, the work looks at how familiar products, languages, smells and everyday exchanges can make an unfamiliar place briefly feel like home. Bringing these fragments together through photographs, wheat-pasted prints and newsprint, the work considers the supermarket not only as a place to buy things, but as a space where familiarity and community are quietly reproduced.

entries.title: things we held and grazed
entries.medium: Photo series, Newsprint and Binder clips
entries.shortDescription: Over fifteen weeks in Chicago, things we held and grazed follows discarded objects left along the streets.
entries.fullText:
Many are things that once came into intimate contact with the body—things we ate from, drank from, held and touched. Some remained in the same place for weeks, each re-encounter more uncanny and begging to be photographed. The work traces these objects after their usefulness has ended, lingering on the strange distance between something once held close and something subsequently left behind.

Things that accompanied us.
Things that fed us.
Things that served us.

Things that we left.
Things that we used.
Things that we forgot.

entries.fullText:
Installation view at [title]Inheritance[/title] (Women in Film and Photography; 2020), Objectifs, Singapore.

Installation view at [title]Inheritance[/title] (Women in Film and Photography; 2020), Objectifs, Singapore.

Developed through improvised darkroom and editing processes, images of coastlines and personal objects are repeatedly copied, altered and recombined until their sources become unstable.
Made while thinking through my Henghua and Singaporean Chinese identity, the work approaches culture in a similar way: not as something fixed or inherited intact, but something continually reproduced and reshaped. The sea recurs throughout the work as both image and method—a form without fixed boundaries, continually changed by movement, contact and return.

entries.title: kuala
entries.shortDescription: 回 kuala begins with a childhood memory of a teapot-shaped landmark on the journey to my father's hometown in Brunei.

presentationHistory.title: CLEANSE: Asia Pacific Now
presentationHistory.venue: Dr Adrian Tan and Desmond Mah

entries.fullText:
I was too young to photograph it then, and more than two decades later, what remains is a vivid but increasingly uncertain image in my mind.

Working with 66 photographs of the landmark found online, I repeatedly process and erode other people's images in an attempt to approach my own. Rather than reconstructing the landmark more clearly, the images become increasingly unstable—somewhere between photographic evidence and remembered image.

回 kuala is an experiment in photographing a memory when a photograph was never taken.

印象深刻的茶壶雕塑在我记忆中是朦胧的。它是跟着我爸爸回汶莱的路上一定会经过的地标。
我记得最后一次看到茶壶应该有二十年前了，听说茶壶的装饰灯已经坏了，时钟也停了。

I remember seeing the teapot over two decades ago, and rumour has it that the lights and clocks on it have already stopped working a few years ago.

entries.title: sync
entries.shortDescription: 默契 sync takes the ritual of pre-concert tuning as a way of thinking about synchronisation within an orchestra.
entries.fullText:
Installation view at [title]How We Learn(t)[/title] (2022), Gillman Barracks, Singapore

Before performing, musicians listen and adjust to one another, producing the impression of a single ensemble coming into tune.
The work separates this collective act into individual measurements. Lines extracted from electronic tuner readings of different orchestras overlap on screen, only occasionally meeting at the “correct” pitch. A five-channel soundtrack resembles an orchestra tuning together, but is assembled from musicians individually tuning their instruments to a machine rather than to one another.
默契  (mò qì, meaning a tacit understanding or rapport) asks how much collective synchronisation is actually shared, and how much is something we perceive or construct.
-

entries.title: who is abing?
entries.shortDescription: 再见阿炳 who is abing?

presentationHistory.title: 印映 reflections impressions
presentationHistory.note: A solo presentation commissioned by Esplanade - Theatres on the Bay. The entire series is an on-going project with further plans to develop it into a book.

entries.fullText:
[title]再见阿炳 who is abing?[/title] begins with the only known surviving photograph of Abing, the influential blind folk musician and erhu player. Despite this single visual reference, his likeness has been repeatedly reimagined through illustrations, sculptures, reenactments and user-made videos.

The work gathers these representations into a continuous strip, tracing how one image has been copied, interpreted and embellished over time. Across them, certain features recur while others drift, contributing to a familiar image of the erhu player that extends beyond Abing himself.

The work considers how a likeness is constructed when there is almost nothing to copy from.

entries.title: phases
entries.shortDescription: 音情圆缺 phases gathers images of the moon found in online videos of Erquan Yingyue (二泉映月, Mirrored Moon in the Erquan Spring).

presentationHistory.title: 印映 reflections impressions
presentationHistory.note: A solo presentation commissioned by Esplanade - Theatres on the Bay. The entire series is an on-going project with further plans to develop it into a book. The audio component is 再现依心曲 ad lib.

entries.fullText:
Across professional performances, amateur recordings and user-made videos, the moon repeatedly appears as a visual shorthand for the music—photographed, illustrated, animated and composited in different ways.
Extracted from their original videos and presented on lightboxes, these moons form a collection of how the same image has been imagined again and again. Like the moon, which is visible through reflected sunlight, these digital moons only appear when illuminated: first by the computer screen, and again by the lightbox.

Like the moon, which is visible through reflected sunlight, these digital moons only appear when illuminated: first by the computer screen, and again by the lightbox.

entries.fullText:
Collaged photographs and texts move between darkroom experiments, family histories, research into the Chinese diaspora in Southeast Asia, and recurring images of the sea.

Rather than resolving these materials into a single account of identity, the book retains the uncertainty of the research process. Images are copied, altered and revisited, while the sea becomes a recurring way of thinking about culture as something inherited yet continually shifting.

Borrowing the words of Kuo Pao Kun, linmo – sketches is just the journal of another "cultural orphan".

entries.fullText:
Enlarged and illuminated, their markings and printing artefacts reveal traces accumulated through use and circulation.
Taking Liu Tianhua's 空山鸟语 (Birdsongs in the Vacant Valley) as a point of departure, these visual traces are also read as graphical scores for new improvisations. Marks that once accompanied the learning and sharing of music are returned to sound, allowing one generation of notation, copying and use to prompt another act of interpretation.

entries.title: 迁泉 shifting springs
entries.shortDescription: 迁泉 shifting springs begins with Huishan's Second Spring (天下第二泉), historically celebrated for the quality of its water for tea and later closely associated with Abing, who played 二泉映月 (Mirrored Moon in the Erquan Spring) there.

presentationHistory.title: A Reservoir of Time
presentationHistory.note: Part of Objectifs' Curator Open Call 2023.

entries.fullText:
Today, the spring has largely dried up, leaving a place whose cultural image persists beyond its water.
The work turns to amateur and professional videos found online, where the spring continues to flow, reappear and be reimagined. Through experimental prints and video objects, these images are processed and displaced, tracing how a place can persist through music, memory and circulating images even as its physical form changes.

泉里的水干了以后，留下的是“白”——空白的白。没有了水，泉反而成了一个可以不断被想象、填补的地方。记忆、音乐和流传的影像在这片空白里交叠，让已经消失的水一次次重新流动。
网上的影像也是如此。不同的人拍摄、上传、转发，又重新想象同一个泉。久而久之，这些影像像一个由大众共同累积的时间囊：泉水或许已经干了，但关于它的想象还在流动。

entries.title: 一笔一勾 in two strokes
entries.shortDescription: 一笔一勾 in two strokes follows the many uses of a simple arrow found across annotated musical scores.
entries.fullText:
A line with a pointed head might indicate phrasing, fingering, rhythm, which note to play, or a change in the order of a passage. Collected across different scores and contexts, the work looks at how an ordinary mark becomes a flexible musical language. I love how something drawn in two strokes can do and mean so much.

entries.title: keeping count
entries.shortDescription: 横竖横竖横 keeping count begins with 正, a five-stroke character commonly used as a tally.
entries.fullText:
In my music notebooks, each stroke marked an instance of practice, slowly completing the character over time.
As a student, I once filled in the tally without having practised. My teacher caught me and remarked that if I continued like this, the only thing I was practising was how to write 正.

This series of 正 takes this reprimand literally. It is a collection of characters written repeatedly in a single sitting, paced against an increasingly fast metronome: practising the act of keeping count rather than the instrument it was meant to account for.

entries.fullText:
ITA_book_1

Made while living away from Singapore, the work follows these spaces through the familiar products, languages, smells and everyday exchanges that briefly made somewhere foreign feel like home.
The work takes the form of a newsprint publication, drawing from the free newspapers and distribution kiosks commonly found in these supermarkets. By borrowing a format already circulating within the space, the book considers the supermarket not only as a place to buy familiar things, but as a place where information, conversation and a sense of community are exchanged.

entries.fullText:
During the pandemic, I took walks around Singapore using Google Maps Street View.

Again and again, patches of pink, magenta and fuchsia appeared at the edges of roads and in my imagined peripheral vision.
Collected into a small accordion book, these images form an affectionate portrait of the bougainvillea scattered throughout Singapore's landscape.

These are the real national flowers of Singapore.

entries.title: chéndiàn; after scans and lingering dust
entries.shortDescription: 尘惦 chéndiàn; after scans and lingering dust begins with hand-copied Chinese music scores repeatedly photocopied for circulation.
entries.fullText:
With each generation, handwritten marks, dust and printing artefacts are copied alongside the music: some traces intensify while others slowly disappear.

The scores are scanned, enlarged, inverted and Risograph printed, turning these incidental traces into images in their own right. Each book contains 43 images selected from a larger set of 127 and is bound to stand upright like a calendar, allowing it to be read slowly over time.

The title plays between 沉淀, to settle or precipitate, and 尘惦, an invented pairing that suggests dust and something that continues to linger in the mind.

沉淀是一个让时间把事物滤清的过程；尘惦则是在尘埃落定后，把依旧惦记在心里的感觉说出来。手抄、手印、手手交换的谱子是一种有迹可循的传承，也是一种由时光冲洗之后，留下的缝隙里的创新和续写。音乐、时间和情感皆是没形没色的，却也是有重量、有着千面百孔的。它们是生动的，是有温度和色彩的。

简谱的字里行间藏有多么多的故事，一笔一画、一点一滴都是不同人留下的印迹与回忆。这一丝丝印迹又再被别人阅览、又再刷上一层釉彩，增添一些质感。反反复复的复印和翻阅把之前的印迹慢慢消化，就如时间把物品消磨成看似细微和单一的尘埃。

Watching dust settle is to witness time passing.

The repeated photocopying of musical scores as a way to share them creates notations of an almost immaterial medium – of dust and artefacts, of music and time. With hand-copied notations, each line and stroke is an imprint and memory left by different people. These traces are read and re-read by others, imbuing a new layer of colour and texture. The repeated acts of copying, reading and sharing slowly erode the previous markings, just like how time wears things down into seemingly minute and homogeneous dust.

entries.title: i’ve never met yoko ono, nor have i touched the sky
entries.medium: Miniature photocards, transparent folder and oversized book belt
entries.shortDescription: 天明日月奣 / i've never met yoko ono, nor have i touched the sky collects images of the sky from photographic documentation of Yoko Ono's Sky TV (1966–2007) and TV to See the Sky (2021).
entries.fullText:
Printed as miniature photocards rather than a fixed sequence, the images can be rearranged, carried, given to a friend or held against the actual sky. The book plays with one of photography's most familiar subjects—the sky that is endlessly photographed.
Its Chinese title borrows an unattributed wordplay in which the characters for sky, sun and moon are rearranged to form 天明日月奣: clear skies, clear skies.

entries.title: what used to be in the mall
entries.shortDescription: what used to be in the mall gathers newspaper clippings about Queensway Shopping Centre from the 1970s to the 1990s.
entries.fullText:
Reports, advertisements and small announcements recall a mall shaped by changing ideas of shopping, nightlife, crime, novelty and entertainment.
Printed on tracing paper and rivet-bound into a small volume, fragments from different decades sit over and through one another. Made as a companion to on telling time in the mall, the book approaches the mall's history through the incidental record left behind in newspapers—what happened there, what was sold there, and what once seemed worth reporting.

entries.fullText:
Many of the source videos, particularly from the 1980s and 1990s, have been copied and reposted repeatedly. Their colours fade, details blur and compression artefacts accumulate, yet the same visual motifs continue to circulate and be reproduced.

about.title: Hong Shu-ying 方舒颖 (b. 1997)
about.artistName: hoards images and stories to make sense of how things are learned and passed on.
about.biography:
Working across moving images, prints, and printed matter, her practice begins with images, notations and other vernacular working documents in circulation. She is interested in the drifts, contradictions and adaptations that allow shared ways of knowing and working to remain legible as they pass through different hands and contexts.

She grew up in amateur Chinese orchestras, where learning took place through photocopied scores, handwritten annotations and imitation. Alongside this, she spent her teenage years collecting and reposting images online. These parallel habits shaped how she looks at vernacular working documents—not simply as records, but as evidence of how information, knowledge and conventions are continually transmitted, adjusted and kept alive through use.

items.text: This curiosity extends beyond the studio. She co-founded Part Time Book Club, an informal collective that expands public access to art books through gatherings and exchanges. In response to limited access to formal residencies and the demands of international travel, she also initiated |      | on paper, a resource-lean residency centred on conversations and four sheets of A4 paper, grounded in the belief that meaningful artistic exchange can grow from modest resources.

Hong Shu-ying received the Kwek Leng Joo Prize of Excellence in Photography and was featured in the 6th Women in Film and Photography Showcase by Objectifs Centre for Photography and Film (SG). She has presented solo exhibitions at Esplanade (SG, 2024) and Yao Alternative Art Space 窯座 (TW, 2024), with an upcoming presentation at RM Gallery (NZ, 2026). Her work has also been shown at Three Shadows Xiamen Photography Art Centre and Pingyao International Photography Festival (CN); Jakarta International Photography Festival (IN); PRINTROOM (NL); CICA Museum (KR); Pon Ding 朋丁 (TW); and DECK, I_S_L_A_N_D_S Peninsula, Art Outreach, and ADM Gallery (SG). She holds a BFA (Hons) in Media Art (Photography) from the School of Art, Design and Media, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore. She was recently a resident at the Singapore Art Museum.

items.title: 1] I think of copying as an imperfect system.
items.text: No copy is ever identical to what came before it, yet copies continue to function. A blurred photocopy remains readable. A contradictory instructional diagram still teaches. A handwritten annotation continues to direct a performance. Rather than treating these differences as failures of reproduction, I am interested in how images and notations keep working through the gaps, mistranslations and contradictions that emerge between copies.

items.title: 2] My work begins with vernacular working documents:
items.text: notations, annotations, instructional diagrams, mass printed media and found images shaped by everyday practices of use. I am drawn to them and hoard them before I know why. They are not neutral records. They carry the traces of circulation and of decisions made to keep them usable. Their surfaces bear the marks of handling, correction, repetition and interpretation, evidence that they have passed through many hands before I held them in mine.

items.title: 3] Rather than extracting them from their original contexts, I borrow from the systems of copying and translation already embedded within them:
items.text: a photocopying protocol, a tracing method, a convention of annotation, a cataloguing system, an indexing structure, a compression standard, an editing strategy, a publishing format.  I work with these documents first as images, reading them photographically even when I no longer use a camera. A flatbed scanner or a screenshot suits this because it refuses the distinction between document and image. A conductor's score, a handwritten note, a GPS photodome and a newspaper clipping all become flat images, entering the same visual field before being reinterpreted through procedures inherited from their own histories.

items.title: 4] This understanding grew from nearly two decades inside amateur Chinese orchestras.
items.text: I eventually served as scores librarian. My role was to maintain the scores cabinet: counting parts, photocopying missing copies, incorporating corrections from rehearsals, and preparing versions that could still be played when we had limited instruments or musicians. Scores were rarely stable. They accumulated annotations, revisions and practical adaptations, sometimes becoming so extensively reworked that they effectively became new master copies.

items.title: 5] Learning rarely took place through pristine scores.
items.text: Techniques were acquired by watching, listening and imitating, and even the notation adapted. In the orchestras I grew up in, we knew a pair of annotation symbols as turtle and dollar sign rather than by their original [Italian] names, because the old names made less sense to a roomful of children learning from borrowed conventions. The symbols stayed useful because the people using them adapted them.

items.title: 6] Meaning does not simply move away from an origin.
items.text: It is continually adjusted by the people who need it to remain usable. What interests me are these quiet acts of maintenance, which let shared systems of knowing and working carry on as they pass through different hands, gathering small contradictions, adaptations and new ways of being understood.
